title: Bebop-era changes: no left hand, no bass drum, experimental harmony
summary: Edison describes how piano, drumming and harmony changed in the bop era and says he often could not understand the new records.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: No. It was worse then than now. Now you wouldn't expect it but then you would expect it, you know. But you had the Bud Powells going then. You had the -- oh, let's see, who else was playing quite a bit around New York? Barry Harris, you had --
Erroll Garner. Oh, you had Dodo Mamarosa, you had all these guys that were playing with the small bands that -- the right hand was coming into common. The left hand

was exactly like the bass drummer's right foot, you know. Went from bass drums to no bass drums. Went from left hand to no left hand. Just that quick. It went from holding one note to making a whole lot of notes on your horn, you know. And it went from making a simple chord to putting a flatted fifth or 13th or suspended note or whatever. It went from the basics to -- of music, to something that people were looking for something. They were trying everything. It was an experimental age in music, I think, because everything was happening.

Some of the records were made I didn't understand. Some of the guys were playing, I couldn't understand what they were playing. I really couldn't. And I never said anything because who's who to say what's right and what's wrong. But if it's not understandable to a musician, how can you have an average person can understand it.
Well, there's always a lot of people who want to appear hip, like a cult. I mean, it's like this Ornette Coleman music--------

Yeah. But some of them I never could understand. I didn't know what they were trying to do. I didn't even know -- I can understand a person striving -- if they haven't arrived yet, you know, it makes sense. But I can't understand a person striving for something that doesn't make sense to improve on it. Because some things you can say, well, he's going to be a bitch when he gets big or something like that, you know. Then

some you'll say, well, I can't ever see where that's going to turn out to be anything, you know. But those that have had quality and those that have contributed something, like the cream will always come to the top, quality will always survive, you know.

Yeah. And I think it's -- they sacrificed the sort of beat you can dance to. And also, there was no -- I mean, if you take something like "Stomping at the Savoy," people when they left the ballroom, they may be only just humming two bars but there was something that stuck in your ear. With that new music, there was nothing for the public really to catch onto, I don't think.
